title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
author: Yu-Hung Wu
Shao-Xiang Yuan
Chan-Hung Yu
Zih-Ching Chen
Kuan-Hao Huang
Shao-Hua Sun
abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning
author: Son Duong
Truong X. Tran
Hai-Anh Tran
abstract: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git

title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
author: Yu Zou
Yan Chen
Jialei Zeng
Xiaorui Zhou
Aixi Zhong
Qi Zhou
Haoran You
Ke Jiang
Changyu Hu
abstract: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
author: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu
abstract:
Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run.
In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens.
Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale.
These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.

title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
author: Seojin Kim
Noseong Park
abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
author: Huy Nghiem
Maria Kostylew
Noam Kolt
abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

title: The ROI of Small Examples: Optimizing In-Context Learning Under Token Budgets
author: Anxo Perez
Jorge GabÃ­n
Javier Parapar
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves large language model performance at inference time without updating model parameters. However, these gains are not free: in practical deployments, longer prompts directly increase inference cost and latency. Under a fixed token budget, prompt construction therefore becomes a resource-allocation problem. While prior work has often focused on how many examples to include in ICL, we study the complementary question of whether the available budget is better spent on a few long demonstrations or on a larger number of shorter ones. We study this aspect in question answering (QA), by organizing candidate demonstrations into length-based bins and constructing prompts from examples within the same length range under fixed budgets. Experiments on two QA benchmarks (\textit{Beat the AI} and \textit{Natural Questions}), using six instruction-tuned LLMs, show that shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space. This effect is especially strong on \textit{Beat the AI}, and remains visible on NQ, although gains are smaller and saturate earlier in the long-context setting. An additional natural language inference experiment on ANLI R3 finds that one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models, although longer demonstrations remain competitive. Overall, our results highlight demonstration granularity as an important factor in prompt design.

title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
author: Hsi Chang
Irfan Khan
abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely ($R^2 > 0.99$) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.

title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
author: Sila Mutaf
Enes YÄ±landiloÄlu
Mohammad Atari
abstract: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

title: EgoPass-Bench: Identifying Objects That May Affect the Wearer's Passage in Egocentric Video
author: Hongyu Wang
Chuhan Li
Congjin Xu
Xuandong Zhao
Hua Shen
abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

title: From Industrial Product Documentation to Automated Digital Product Passport Generation: An Experimental Study of Large Language Models
author: Marco Buecheler
Grant Richards
Nathan Hartman
abstract: Manufacturing companies that are planning to sell certain products in the European Union (EU) will be required to provide mandatory digital product passports (DPPs). The use of DPPs is to provide standardized product information throughout multiple product life cycles in a circular economy. Required passport information, such as technical specifications, material composition, and environmental product footprint, is available in manufacturers' data sources but is scattered across different heterogeneous systems, documents, and data formats. The given paper investigates using large language models (LLMs) to automate the generation of DPPs based on the asset administration shell (AAS). A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach is used to extract product information from industrial documentation and generate populated AAS instances. Product documentation is processed and divided into text chunks. The text chunks are then stored in a persistent ChromaDB vector database using vector embeddings. The retrieval process combines semantic and lexical search to identify relevant information based on standardized AAS submodel template requirements. The retrieved information is provided to five LLMs to generate structured AAS instances. The experiments cover different industrial products and AAS submodels. Four levels of prompt guidance are investigated to assess their influence on generation quality. The generated passports are evaluated against a ground truth. The experimental evaluation includes 4,560 executions across 76 product-submodel combinations. Of the generated passport outputs, 97.4% are valid JSON, while 44.9% pass the full AAS validation procedure. Under deterministic scoring, mean completeness, conditional accuracy, and overall field correctness are 49.6%, 58.3%, and 30.8%, respectively. An LLM-as-a-judge yields better scores of 66.5%, 88.9%, and 60.4% for the same outputs.

title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
author: Ido Nitzan Hidekel
Dan Raviv
abstract:
Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.
At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.
Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

title: Attacks and Defenses in Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Hop-by-Hop Task Decomposition and Delegation
author: Matthew D. Laws
Maria Lazou
Alina Oprea
Cristina Nita-Rotaru
abstract:
Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents.
In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.

title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
author: Jiaru Qian
Jiawei Li
Xiaolong Hu
Zheng Shen
LiMing Zhao
Xin Zhang
Siyuan Jiang
Yongqiang Wei
Dong Liu
Jianyang Li
Yihua Chen
Yangxu Liao
Yuxin Wu
Jing Liang
Bin Wen
Junjie Zhang
Yongsheng Han
Yihong Dong
Ge Li
abstract: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.

title: Mapping the Wind to Find the Source: Online Physics-Informed Gas Source Localization with Mobile Robots
author: Wanting Jin
Thomas Wiedemann
Han Fan
Achim Lilienthal
Alcherio Martinoli
abstract: Gas Source Localization (GSL) with mobile robots is challenging because wind and gas measurements are spatially sparse, noisy, and potentially affected by robot motion. Indoor airflow can vary substantially across space, while detailed environmental layouts, boundary conditions, or precomputed airflow fields are often unavailable. Moreover, hazardous sources must be localized as quickly as possible, making exhaustive exploration impractical. This paper presents a lightweight physics-informed probabilistic framework for efficient GSL under spatially varying indoor airflow. As the robot navigates, it continuously collects wind and gas measurements and reconstructs the spatially varying airflow field online. The estimated wind field drives a forward dispersion model that predicts the gas pattern for each candidate source location. These predictions are compared with the measured gas pattern to update a probabilistic belief over the source location. As the wind field is reconstructed incrementally, the framework also accounts for the spatially non-uniform reliability of wind field estimation and its influence on the source estimation. The resulting belief map is then used for informative path planning to guide the robot toward informative regions. High-fidelity simulations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the individual components and their integrations within the complete system, while physical indoor experiments assess the system performance under realistic sensing, motion, and airflow conditions. The results demonstrate that incorporating lightweight physical knowledge significantly improves localization robustness under spatially complex airflow and enables more efficient exploration.

title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
author: Haoran Xu
Tian Chen
Yuhe Wu
Yanbo Zhao
Junchi Liao
Hongyu Wang
Jiaze Li
Wentao Wang
Yanfeng Li
Rui Qian
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kaelyn01/VisAlloc

title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
author: Nianjun Zhou
Dhaval Patel
abstract:
This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts.
A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
author: Meenakshi Rajpurohit
Anna Phan
Ravikumar Komandur Narayanan
Gunanidhi Ramakrishnan
Nathan Howland
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

title: Twindex: Index Cache Offloading with Coarse-to-Fine Selection for Long-Context Sparse-Attention Serving
author: Yuxuan Xia
Jiakun Fan
Han Meng
Hao Mark Chen
Shenji Wan
Dongsheng Yang
abstract: In long-context decoding, GPU memory (HBM) caps how many requests a GPU decodes at once. Sparse-attention models such as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 add an indexer: at every step it scores all past index entries with its own indexer cache, and attention reads the main KV of only the top-k entries. We find that once serving systems move the main KV to host memory, the indexer cache becomes the HBM bottleneck, at 63% of per-request HBM on Qwen and 75% on V4.1 at 1M tokens. Therefore, we introduce Twindex, which keeps only a compact copy of the indexer cache in HBM and the full indexer cache in host memory. At each step, the copy selects a larger candidate set, and the model's own indexer picks the top-k from the original rows of the candidates in host memory. The copy combines the shared component with the compressed residuals, both learned once offline. Twindex changes no model weights and runs inside CUDA graphs. At 1M tokens on modern GPUs, Twindex fits $1.78\times$, $1.62\times$ and $3.03\times$ as many requests as KV offloading alone on Qwen, V4.1 and GLM-5.2, and reaches $1.44\times$, $1.25\times$ and $2.54\times$ decode throughput when host memory does not limit the batch. Every request keeps its own index, and Qwen and GLM requests share prefix main KV in host memory. In our evaluations, mean benchmark scores are at most 3.1% below the baseline's.

title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
author: Mohammadali Khodabandehlou
Mahdi Alizadeh
Lei Gao
Murali Annavaram
Bhaskar Krishnamachari
abstract: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7-3.5x the best-effort throughput of the strongest ones; beside LLM serving, it meets per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running. Sharing a closed GPU under SLOs needs no new preemption mechanism, only control over what the existing one sees.

title: HapBO: Harnessed $Î±$-$Ï$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
author: Jean-SÃ©bastien Giroux
Rose Guay Hottin
Marco Bonizzato
abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
author: Xianzhe Fan
Chi-Pin Huang
Fu-En Yang
Jing Wang
Yecheng Wu
Yu-Cheng Chou
Johan Bjorck
Linxi "Jim" Fan
Jan Kautz
Yu-Chiang Frank Wang
Zhiding Yu
Hengshuang Zhao
Zhiqi Li
abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
author: Shwetanshu Singh
Mark Keavney
Mathieu Duteil
Meriem Mehri
Scott Blain
abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
author: Junfeng Nie
Xiaohui Chen
abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.

title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect -- KV Cache Management for AI Agents
author: Shashwat Jaiswal
Chloe Alverti
Mengmei Ye
Chen Wang
Hubertus Franke
Fan Lai
Tianyin Xu
Josep Torrellas
abstract:
LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference.
To address this problem, we present \emph{TripleKV}, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. %exploits tool execution to hide these delays. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory.
Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45--76\% to under 10\%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49\% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
author: Ziyan Yang
Taiwei Shi
Jieyu Zhao
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

title: CRAFT: Constrained Route planning with Adaptive Framework and Template-based code generation
author: Shahd Elmahallawy
Ahmed Eldawy
abstract: Everyday routing requests are rarely a point-to-point shortest path. A driver may need to visit stops, sometimes in a fixed order, under time budgets or distance limits, and perhaps recharge their EV car along the way. Each combination is a distinct routing problem that classically requires its own algorithm, so no fixed solver covers the space of queries users may ask. This paper presents CRAFT, which takes a constrained routing query as free text and returns a route that satisfies the user's requirements on a real road network. An LLM parses the query and generates four search functions, which a generic graph-search engine executes on the road network. We formalize the underlying problem as State-Expanded RCSP (SE-RCSP), which extends resource-constrained shortest paths (RCSP) with non-additive state such as node-dependent resets and discrete progress tracking. We evaluate CRAFT on 2,600 natural-language queries over California road networks against two baselines, analyzing correctness, constraint violations, long-distance scalability, and semantic POI filtering.

title: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
author: Rudransh Agnihotri
Manasvi Kapoor
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.

title: Asymmetric rhetorical strategies drive partisanship in television news
author: Upasana Dutta
Homa Hosseinmardi
Amir Ghasemian
Aaron Clauset
Duncan J. Watts
abstract: Television remains a dominant source of political information in the United States, yet systematic evidence on how partisanship is expressed in televised news remains limited. Prior research has largely treated partisanship as a one-dimensional construct, offering limited insight into the rhetorical strategies that underlie ideological bias. Here, by analyzing over 400,000 news episodes using large language models (LLMs), we provide a multi-dimensional measure of partisanship bias in television news across six major U.S. news stations (2013--2025). We identify eight interpretable linguistic features that explain 73% of partisanship variance in television news.\ Our findings reveal systematic asymmetries across stations. While MSNBC and CNN shifted leftward during Republican presidencies and moderated under Democratic presidencies, Fox News increased its conservative alignment following each election regardless of the electoral outcome. Beyond aggregate trends, MSNBC and CNN emphasized attacks on Republican actors more than reinforcement of Democratic positions, whereas Fox News reinforced Republican viewpoints substantially more than it attacked Democratic viewpoints. The association between in-group praise and out-group attacks was also threefold stronger on Fox News than on MSNBC. These results are validated against trained human raters and replicated with four additional LLMs with differing political leanings. Together, our study reveals systematic station-level differences in the rhetorical strategies with which ideological slant is communicated in television news, opening new opportunities for future research on media effects, audience attitudes, and political communication.

title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
author: Fangrui Huang
Bingyang Wang
Chuhan Li
Yijiang Li
Arpandeep Khatua
Austin Shen
Riki R Z Choi
Cuiyuanxiu Chen
Jin Huang
Zachary Robertson
Kate Lin
Akshay Paruchuri
Sijun Tan
Xin Liu
Zhengmin Ni
Sanmi Koyejo
Ehsan Adeli
abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

title: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
author: Yunye Gong
Indranil Sur
Jared Claypoole
Pritish Sahu
Ajay Divakaran
abstract: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.

title: Robust BUG dynamical low-rank integrators based on the Euler-Maruyama method for stochastic differential equations. Part I: a closed-moment approach
author: SÃ©bastien Riffaud
abstract: In this work, we introduce Euler-Maruyama-based Basis-Update & Galerkin (EM-BUG) dynamical low-rank integrators for stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These integrators extend the standard BUG integrator to the Euler-Maruyama scheme by incorporating diffusion directions into the augmented physical basis and exploiting the second moment to update the physical basis independently of the new Brownian increments. This construction avoids the inversion of the reduced second-moment matrix and allows us to derive convergence estimates that are robust with respect to small eigenvalues. We establish preservation of positive semidefiniteness, exactness with respect to Euler-Maruyama at full rank, and second-moment stability. Strong and weak convergence estimates show that the time-discretization accuracy of the underlying Euler-Maruyama scheme is preserved up to the low-rank approximation error. We also derive Monte Carlo error estimates recovering the standard sampling rate up to the time-discretization and low-rank approximation errors. Numerical experiments on linear SDEs with additive and multiplicative noise support these theoretical results and demonstrate accuracy comparable to the standard BUG integrator.

title: GridAnchor: Specialized Multi-Agent AI for Safeguarding Autonomous Energy Systems Against Cyber-Physical Hallucinations
author: Abderaouf Bahi
Hasan Masrur
abstract: Autonomous energy systems increasingly chain specialized learned agents, such as a forecaster, a state estimator and a dispatcher that may be a language model. These agents can emit confident outputs that contradict physics, and downstream agents may act on them. We define such cyber-physical hallucinations and their cascades, organize them in eight types, and build CPH-Bench, a generator of labeled episodes on SimBench feeders. We propose GridAnchor, a verification layer whose Physics-Residual Graph Transformer scores every claim from residuals between the claims, the measurements and a linearized grid model. Mondrian conformal p-values with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure turn the scores into decisions, a root head attributes cascades, and a quadratic program repairs unsafe actions with a voltage margin calibrated at repaired steps. On a simulated rural medium-voltage feeder, GridAnchor reaches a message-level area under the precision-recall curve of 0.846, against 0.837 for the strongest of six baselines, a difference within the confidence interval. It leads on estimates and actions, whereas a self-consistency check that knows the label tolerances reaches 0.874 by leading on forecasts. The false-alarm rate stays within 0.17 percentage points of the nominal level on steps without injected hallucinations. In closed loop, GridAnchor leaves no bus outside the voltage band on the test days, against 0.0700% of the bus-steps without protection, and simpler detectors with the same mitigation come close. Stale but coherent messages and single-bus forecast errors remain mostly undetected.

title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
author: Anh Tien Nguyen
Dimitris Samaras
Mahdi S. Hosseini
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations
author: Zhiwen Qiu
Daisy Lin
Diyu Zhou
Jialin Wu
Rosita Ji
Saleh Kalantari
abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.

title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
author: Mark Lovett
Denis Lim
Soroush Vosoughi
abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
author: Zirui Song
Jiadong Zhang
Zheng Lu
Xiaosong Ma
Xiaojun Chang
Xiuying Chen
abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

title: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
author: Liang Yue
Eric A. Vance
abstract: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels. A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
author: Luca M. Hartmann
Parinaz Naghizadeh
abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

title: VG-Steer: Visual-Geometric Policy Steering from In-Context Aligned Abstractions
author: Arthur Bucker
Pramod Anantharam
Jonathan Francis
Jean Oh
abstract: Adapting robot policies to out-of-distribution (OOD) settings with limited real-world data remains a key bottleneck to generalist robots. The multimodality and scarcity of robotics data lead end-to-end approaches to overfit and break under small distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation can alleviate this by correcting frozen policies at inference, but most methods ground their correction in a signal learned implicitly from robotic datasets, making it susceptible to the same shifts as the policy it corrects. Recent methods that instead exploit explicit spatial information are typically limited to coarse corrections, missing the nuanced, task-relevant motion most manipulation tasks require. We propose VG-Steer, which corrects existing policies by transferring the nuanced motion of successful in-distribution rollouts, captured along meaningful geometric axes, known here as object-relational distance pairs. VG-Steer leverages the semantic understanding of Large Vision Models (LVMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reasoning, which combines the task-relevant entity pairs and their object-relational distance projections into a single tailored visual-geometric guidance signal. In a simulation benchmark, it efficiently corrects flow-matching policies under pose and task-goal shifts; on a real robot experiment, it widens the region of the workspace the frozen policy covers, more than doubling its success rate on cable placements one grid step outside the training positions, and steers a single-task policy toward objects it was never trained on while nearly eliminating object confusion. Project website: https://arthurfenderbucker.github.io/VG-Steer/

title: ÏTD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
author: Thomas Mousseau
Tyler Kastner
Davide Baldelli
Amir-massoud Farahmand
abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

title: Recurrent Vision Language Models Solve the Shell Game
author: Dingqiang Ye
Jiacong Xu
Wen Zhang
Yiqun Mei
Vishal M. Patel
abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.

title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
author: Jeonghoon Lee
abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.

title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
author: Fangxu Yu
Tao Feng
Xuying Ning
Haolin Yang
Jiaxuan You
Tianyi Zhou
abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.

title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
author: Takahiro Miki
Robin Schmid
Manthan Patel
Turcan Tuna
Julia Richter
Julian Nubert
Joonho Lee
Matthias MÃ¼ller
Marco Hutter
abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
author: Anima Singh
Suhas Yogin
Weicheng Kuo
Ivor Rendulic
Ivan Jurin
Antoine Yang
Oran Kelly
Rohan Doshi
Hammad Ayyubi
Ioana Bica
Sergi Caelles
Matthew Conniff
Dan Graur
Anastasija IliÄ
Ahmet Iscen
Chao Jia
Tomasz KÄpa
Chunyuan Li
Noah Ã Donnaile
Filip Pavetic
Goran Petrovic
Khalid Salama
Zhicheng Wang
Polina Zablotskaia
Yiqian Zhang
Ming Zhao
Benjamin Caine
Mario LuÄiÄ
Melvin Johnson
Radu Soricut
Jean-Baptiste Alayrac
abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP$.$pdf and GDP$.$xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
author: Haochen Liu
Guanghui Min
Song Wang
Yada Zhu
Chen Chen
Jundong Li
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.

title: Ferrofluid Shape Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning
author: Anthony Czubarow
Antonio Terpin
Raffaello D'Andrea
abstract: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium.
